description: Paired case studies showing the same incident from two viewpoints: a traditional log-only stack (Splunk/CloudWatch/syslog) and the eBPF/Tetragon/Hubble view that ships with kldload. Each section is a real incident pattern — the left panel is what you'd see with logs alone, the right panel is what eBPF reveals about WHY it happened.

options.content:
## eBPF — why kldload was built on it

Every row below shows the **same incident** twice. Left side is what a **traditional log-only stack** (any SIEM, syslog forwarder, or cloud logging tier) lets you see. Right side is what a kernel-level eBPF view sees about the same moment in time.

Both panels read **live from this kldload box**. The pattern: traditional logging tells you *what* happened. eBPF tells you *why* — at kernel-function granularity, with no agent install, no separate license, no app instrumentation.

**Storage and disk operations get particular attention** here because kldload was originally built as a test bench for OpenZFS at scale — every panel related to block I/O, fsync, txg, or ARC behaviour is wired to surface things `iostat` and log scraping can't.

panels.title: Case 1 — "Disk feels slow" (the ZFS testbench origin story)

options.content:
**Scenario.** An application, pod, or VM reports a slow file open, slow query, or I/O timeout. A baseline disk dashboard confirms that average wait time has risen.

The average alone does not identify the cause. The wait could be hardware degradation, a noisy neighbour, page-cache eviction, a ZFS scrub, a txg sync, an ARC cold-miss, or a single application issuing pathological I/O. Each hypothesis requires a separate investigation when the only signal is an aggregate.

The two panels below show the same workload through two methods.

**Left** — the average. Produced by polling `/proc/diskstats` and computing a rate over a 1-minute window. This is the signal a Splunk Disk app, a Loki host-exporter dashboard, or a Dynatrace Host Disk module displays. It identifies that latency has risen.

**Right** — every individual block I/O request, plotted by the time it took to complete. The shape of the distribution narrows the cause: a single outlier row identifies one slow request; two bright bands identify a cache-miss pattern; persistent heat in the top row during a scrub identifies noisy-neighbour I/O.

Panel descriptions below each chart document what the view can and cannot see, the data path, and the CLI tool that produces the same numbers for ad-hoc work.

panels.title: Traditional view — averaged disk wait time
panels.description:
NAME
    Traditional view — averaged disk wait time

DESCRIPTION
    Per-device average request wait + service time, in seconds, over
    the most-recent 1-minute window. The same number iostat(8) -x
    reports in the `await` column.

EQUIVALENT IN OTHER TOOLS
    Splunk Stream — Disk Performance app, `disk_io_wait_time` field.
    Loki / host-exporter — same Prometheus counter rendered as a
        time-series.
    Dynatrace — Host Disk module, `Average wait time` metric.
    All compute the same aggregate from the same kernel-emitted
    cumulative counter.

SOURCE
    node_exporter reads /proc/diskstats every scrape interval (15s
    default) and exposes cumulative counters:
        node_disk_io_time_weighted_seconds_total
        node_disk_io_time_seconds_total
    Query:
        rate(io_time_weighted[1m]) / rate(io_time[1m])

FIELDS
    < 1 ms      NVMe under healthy load.
    < 10 ms     SATA SSD under healthy load.
    < 50 ms     Spinning rust under load, healthy.
    Steady values are normal. A rising trend without a workload
    increase warrants investigation.

CAVEATS
    The aggregation discards information present in the source data:
        Individual request outliers are averaged out.
        Read and write are combined in the source counter.
        Sync and async I/O are combined.
        The process or dataset that issued the request is not
            recorded by this counter.
        Queue time and service time are combined.
        On ZFS, txg, scrub, ARC-fill, and application I/O are
            combined into one number.
    A bimodal workload (50% of requests at 1 ms, 50% at 9 ms) reports
    as 5 ms — indistinguishable from a uniform 5 ms workload.

SEE ALSO
    Panel to the right — per-request heatmap. Resolves every item
        listed under CAVEATS.
    iostat(8) -x — the CLI form of this metric.
    Documentation/admin-guide/iostats.rst — kernel source for the
        underlying counters.

panels.title: kldload view — kernel block-layer latency per request (eBPF)
panels.description:
NAME
    kldload view — kernel block-layer latency per request (eBPF)

DESCRIPTION
    Heatmap of every block I/O request the kernel completed in the
    most-recent 1-minute window, binned by service time on a
    power-of-two microsecond scale. Cell brightness encodes the rate
    of requests in that latency bucket.

EQUIVALENT IN OTHER TOOLS
    None. Splunk and Loki ingest log lines emitted by applications;
    Dynatrace agents sample running processes at a configured
    interval (10s default). None of these observe individual
    block-layer requests at the kernel boundary. The closest
    commercial equivalent is Splunk Stream's per-IOP collector,
    which still aggregates to time-window averages before display.

SOURCE
    BPF program at /etc/ebpf_exporter/biolatency.yaml, attached as
    a kretprobe on blk_account_io_done() in block/blk-core.c. Each
    request's elapsed service time is recorded in a
    BPF_MAP_TYPE_HISTOGRAM named bio_latency. ebpf_exporter reads
    the map every 5s and exposes:
        ebpf_exporter_bio_latency_seconds_bucket{le="..."}
    Query:
        sum by (le) (rate(...bio_latency_seconds_bucket[1m]))

FIELDS
    The brightest row identifies device class:
        64 - 256 us     NVMe steady state.
        256 us - 2 ms   SATA SSD, or NVMe under queue-depth pressure.
        2 - 16 ms       Spinning rust, healthy.
        16 - 128 ms     Spinning rust under contention or scrub.
    Two bright bands (bimodal distribution) indicate ZFS ARC misses
        falling to a slower vdev tier.
    Persistent heat in the top row during a scrub identifies the
        scrub I/O without correlating to zpool status.
    A right-shift over time without a workload change is the
        canonical early indicator of a failing SSD.

CAVEATS
    Counts requests with a usable device pointer. Some device-mapper
        targets (dm-flakey, certain dm-cache modes) strip this and
        do not appear here.
    Software RAID (md) requests appear twice — once for the array,
        once per leg — inflating totals relative to physical I/O.
    The kretprobe does not fire on I/O completed in interrupt
        context that bypasses blk_account_io_done. This affects
        certain NVMe polling modes; uncommon on default kernels.

SEE ALSO
    Panel to the left — same workload, aggregated.
    /usr/share/bcc/tools/biolatency — CLI form, prints the same
        histogram to a terminal.
    /usr/share/bcc/tools/biosnoop — per-request log with PID and
        command name. Identifies the process that issued a slow
        request.
    zfs_arc_hits / zfs_arc_misses panels — confirms whether bimodal
        heat is ARC-miss-driven.

panels.title: Case 2 — Pod can't reach a service

options.content:
**The symptom**: pod logs say `connection refused` or `i/o timeout`.

**Traditional reporting** counts the error log lines. From there the cause is one of: NetworkPolicy, missing route, MTU mismatch, DNS, overlay encapsulation, the target pod actually being down. Each takes a different operator to disprove.

**kldload's eBPF view** (Hubble) lives in the kernel datapath itself. Every dropped flow is annotated with the verdict, the policy that did it, the source + destination identity, and the L4/L7 layer. No guessing — the kernel says exactly what it did.

panels.title: Traditional view — application log error rate
panels.description: Loki rate of pod / journal lines containing connection-error keywords. Tells you failures are happening; cannot tell you whether it's NetworkPolicy, MTU, DNS, or that the remote pod actually died. Requires that the application logs the error in the first place (many connection-pool wrappers don't).

panels.title: kldload view — Hubble flow drops by kernel verdict
panels.description: `hubble_drop_total` — every L3/L4/L7 flow eBPF observed dropping in the kernel, broken out by drop verdict. `POLICY_DENIED` = a NetworkPolicy did it. `UNDEFINED` = no policy covers this identity pair. `MISSED_TAIL_CALL` = MTU or fragmentation. The traditional error spike on the left aligns to the second with one of these verdicts on the right — that's root cause, not symptom.

options.content:
**The symptom**: kubelet restarts a pod with exit code 137.

**Traditional reporting** counts restarts. It cannot tell you whether the pod was OOM-killed, kernel-killed, runtime-killed, or self-exited cleanly. It also cannot tell you *when in the resource curve* the kill happened — was the pod climbing toward a limit, hit it fast, or get killed because a different process on the node went haywire?

**kldload's eBPF view** sees the actual `node_vmstat_oom_kill` counter (a SIGKILL the kernel's OOM killer issued) alongside the `MemAvailable` curve leading up to it. The curve climbing toward zero right before the kill is the smoking gun. Pair with Tetragon's `process_exit` event to get the exact PID.

panels.title: Traditional view — kubelet pod-start error counter
panels.description: `kubelet_started_pods_errors_total` — a flat counter of "pod start failed" events as the kubelet sees them. Tells you how many pods failed; says nothing about why (OOM vs image pull vs network vs runtime). On a log-only stack this is what you have to work with.

panels.title: kldload view — OOM kills + memory available trend
panels.description: Top line = `node_vmstat_oom_kill` (every actual SIGKILL the kernel's OOM killer issued). Bottom line = `MemAvailable / MemTotal` (fraction of usable memory free). The available curve dives toward zero right before the kill — you can see it coming. Pair with `tetragon_events_total{event="process_exit",signal="SIGKILL"}` to confirm the exact PID and command-line at the kill instant.

panels.title: Case 4 — Permission denied (on what, by whom?)

options.content:
**The symptom**: an application or operator gets `EACCES` / `EPERM` from a syscall.

**Traditional reporting** records the string "permission denied" in an application log. It does not name which file, which UID, which capability, or which LSM (SELinux / AppArmor / cap_check) said no — and it cannot say whether the syscall was `open()`, `mount()`, `bind()`, or one of forty others.

**kldload's eBPF view** (Tetragon) traces every syscall the kernel handles. With a TracingPolicy filtering `returnCode < 0` on `security_file_open`, every deny is captured with PID, parent PID, process name, file path, capability flags, and return code. The deny IS the event — no log scraping required.

panels.title: Traditional view — log lines mentioning permission denied
panels.description: Loki tail on systemd-journal + kldload-apps for any line containing "permission denied" / "EACCES" / "EPERM". Timestamp + a free-text string. No path argument, no actor PID, no LSM context.

panels.title: eBPF view — Tetragon kernel events (msg_op breakdown)
panels.description: Tetragon publishes one Prometheus counter per BPF event class. `msg_op=5` EXECVE (every process exec the kernel saw). `msg_op=7` EXIT (every process exit + signal, including OOM SIGKILLs). `msg_op=23` PROCESS_KPROBE (every kernel function call your TracingPolicies trace — file opens, capability checks, syscall returns). The deny the traditional log says "EACCES" about IS in `msg_op=23` with the full kernel context (PID, path argument, return code, security labels). Volume alone tells you Tetragon is observing thousands of syscalls per second without measurable cost.

panels.title: Case 5 — CPU spike of unknown origin

options.content:
**The symptom**: load average climbs, the app gets sluggish, `top` shows one process at 200% CPU but won't say what it's doing.

**Traditional reporting** captures load average and per-process CPU time. It cannot break those down into the syscall flavours that drove them — runaway forks, kqueue thrash, page-fault storm, syscall flood, kernel-side BPF tax all look the same in user CPU columns.

**kldload's eBPF view** splits the kernel's actual time across BPF programs by program name (so you know which observer is hot) AND across user-space processes by groupname (so you know which user workload is hot). Two lines, two layers of attribution, one panel.

panels.title: Traditional view — system load average
panels.description: `node_load1` — 1-minute load average. Tells you the system is busy. Says nothing about user vs kernel time, which subsystem, which syscall family, or whether the load is from observability tooling itself.

panels.title: kldload view — kernel BPF program time + user-space process time
panels.description: Top series: BPF program time/second per program (the kernel-side cost of observability — if Tetragon is hot, it's named here, by program). Bottom series: user-space CPU per process group (the workload-side cost). Together they tell you which side of the kernel/user boundary is driving the load — something `top` and `htop` cannot do.

options.content:
---

### Why kldload ships these dashboards in the box

Traditional logging is an after-the-fact summary of what your code wrote down. eBPF is the kernel telling you what it actually did. Same incident, two categories of signal — the second one names root cause instead of describing symptoms.

kldload was built as a test bench for OpenZFS at scale, and the test matrix kept catching regressions that averaged metrics hid. Every panel on this page is something we needed to see — and once it was wired, it turned out to be useful for every other workload too. **You get the lab, not a marketing demo.**

No agent install, no separate license, no upgrade tier. Just the box.
